modes.ritualCard:
No audience, no confetti. What still survives?
Imagine quietly stopping. Who appears first in your mind looking disappointed, impressed, confused or relieved? Name them. Ask what you would still want if nobody ever found out.
Guess whose reaction matters most if you imagine quitting the goal tomorrow.
Notice the gap between the audience goal and the private goal.
modes.goal: Let’s check whether this goal is yours or merely renting space in your calendar.
modes.rule: Guess whose reaction matters most if you imagine quitting the goal tomorrow.
modes.play: Imagine quietly stopping. Who appears first in your mind looking disappointed, impressed, confused or relieved? Name them. Ask what you would still want if nobody ever found out.
modes.twist: Notice the gap between the audience goal and the private goal.
modes.mindBend: If nobody could clap, what would still be worth doing?
modes.why: Approval can power a goal without making the goal personally meaningful.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Let the mental image create possibilities, not excuses. Keep direct words, consent, patterns of behaviour and your own boundaries in the picture. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

Pick a continuous sound: aircon, traffic, hum, rain, fridge. Listen only for the first change in pitch, volume, rhythm or distance.
Guess how long it will stay exactly the same.
Catch the moment “constant” becomes obviously variable.
modes.goal: Choose one sound and wait for it to betray its own sameness.
modes.rule: Guess how long it will stay exactly the same.
modes.play: Pick a continuous sound: aircon, traffic, hum, rain, fridge. Listen only for the first change in pitch, volume, rhythm or distance.
modes.twist: Catch the moment “constant” becomes obviously variable.
modes.mindBend: What feels continuous is often changing underneath your label for it.
modes.why: Attention reveals micro-changes that a stressed brain compresses into “this is just how it is.”
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example to one brief experiment. If it starts making you less steady, more confused or more stuck, stop and return to the concrete facts in front of you. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

modes.openingLine: Your skin ran the experiment. No lab coat needed.
modes.characterLine: Your skin ran the experiment. No lab coat needed.
modes.ritualCard:
Your skin ran the experiment. No lab coat needed.
Touch a safe cool or warm object for one second. Remove it. Count slowly until the sensation changes category—strong to mild, sharp to vague, local to spread.
Guess how many seconds the strongest sensation will last.
Compare the predicted duration with the actual change point.
modes.goal: Touch something cool or warm and make a prediction before your skin votes.
modes.rule: Guess how many seconds the strongest sensation will last.
modes.play: Touch a safe cool or warm object for one second. Remove it. Count slowly until the sensation changes category—strong to mild, sharp to vague, local to spread.
modes.twist: Compare the predicted duration with the actual change point.
modes.mindBend: A sensation can be intense without being stable.
modes.why: Body sensations are dynamic, and prediction often overestimates how fixed they will feel.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use only comfortably mild temperatures and brief skin contact—no ice, very hot objects or prolonged exposure. Stop with pain, numbness, burning, or a lasting change in skin colour.

PAUSE

Body weather report. No opinion column.
Notice your pulse, chest, throat or stomach. Describe only physical properties: fast, slow, tight, warm, fluttery, heavy, moving. No “anxious,” “bad,” “dangerous,” or “because.”
Guess whether you can describe the sensation without using an emotion word.
Catch how quickly the mind tries to add an explanation.
modes.goal: Find a body signal and ban the biography for ten seconds.
modes.rule: Guess whether you can describe the sensation without using an emotion word.
modes.play: Notice your pulse, chest, throat or stomach. Describe only physical properties: fast, slow, tight, warm, fluttery, heavy, moving. No “anxious,” “bad,” “dangerous,” or “because.”

modes.mindBend: Your body can send a signal before your story decides what it means.
modes.why: Sensation and interpretation arrive close together, but they are not the same event.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Do one short observation only; repeated symptom checking can feed the loop. Concerning or persistent physical symptoms are for medical assessment, not self-reassurance.

Every highlight has laundry somewhere off-camera.
Picture the highlight you envy. Now widen the crop: morning mess, waiting, admin, or similar. Add only possibilities, not accusations.
Guess what invisible material must exist outside the frame of the person you are comparing yourself with.
Notice how the comparison changes when the frame becomes less selective.
modes.goal: You are comparing your full camera roll with someone else’s selected thumbnail.
modes.rule: Guess what invisible material must exist outside the frame of the person you are comparing yourself with.
modes.play: Picture the highlight you envy. Now widen the crop: morning mess, waiting, admin, or similar. Add only possibilities, not accusations.
modes.twist: Notice how the comparison changes when the frame becomes less selective.
modes.mindBend: You cannot fairly compare your behind-the-scenes with somebody else’s trailer.
modes.why: Comparison is distorted when one side includes backstage footage and the other side contains only the poster.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the mental image to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.

modes.openingLine: Receipt lost. Compliment stays.
modes.characterLine: Receipt lost. Compliment stays.
modes.ritualCard:
Receipt lost. Compliment stays.
Recall or receive one genuine compliment. Your only allowed response is “thank you.” No joke, discount, counterexample, explanation or compliment-back for 10 sec.
Guess how quickly you will feel the urge to explain why the compliment does not count.
Catch the exact urge to return the positive information.
modes.goal: For ten seconds, compliments are non-refundable.
modes.rule: Guess how quickly you will feel the urge to explain why the compliment does not count.
modes.play: Recall or receive one genuine compliment. Your only allowed response is “thank you.” No joke, discount, counterexample, explanation or compliment-back for 10 sec.
modes.twist: Catch the exact urge to return the positive information.
modes.mindBend: Sometimes praise feels wrong because your self-image has an outdated returns policy.
modes.why: The discomfort may be the old self-story defending itself, not proof the compliment is false.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the simple thank-you only for a genuine, welcome compliment. You do not need to accept praise, contact or attention that feels inappropriate, unsafe or boundary-crossing.

modes.ritualCard:
One no. Please do not let it purchase a billboard.
Say only the fact: “They said no to ___.” Then list the bigger meanings your mind added.
Guess how many extra claims were added after the actual refusal.
Count how many conclusions were not literally contained in the original no.
modes.goal: One “no” is trying to write a biography about you.
modes.rule: Guess how many extra claims were added after the actual refusal.
modes.play: Say only the fact: “They said no to ___.” Then list the bigger meanings your mind added.
modes.twist: Count how many conclusions were not literally contained in the original no.
modes.mindBend: “No to this” and “no to you as a human” are different sentences.
modes.why: A refusal can be painful and specific at the same time.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the sentence on the interpretation, not the other person's rights or limits. A kinder explanation does not cancel a clear no, repeated harm or needed distance. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

Set 10 sec. Think of the unanswered message, quiet room or pause. For the full 10 sec, every time meaning appears—angry, bored, rejecting—replace it with 1 word: “silence.”
Guess what your brain will try to make silence mean first.
Catch how aggressively the mind tries to turn absence of information into information.
modes.goal: Silence gets ten seconds without being forced to explain itself.
modes.rule: Guess what your brain will try to make silence mean first.

modes.twist: Catch how aggressively the mind tries to turn absence of information into information.
modes.mindBend: Silence is empty data. Your brain hates leaving the field blank.
modes.why: Ambiguity feels unfinished, so the brain often completes it with whatever fits the current mood.
modes.safety:
PAUSE

Check if the loud sound changed—or whether your attention changed its rank.

modes.rule: Pick the loudest sound. Guess whether it still feels dominant after you deliberately promote a quieter sound.

modes.twist: Check if the loud sound changed—or whether your attention changed its rank.
modes.mindBend: You do not always need silence; sometimes you need a different foreground.
modes.why: Sensory dominance is partly about volume and partly about where attention points.
modes.safety:
PAUSE

Check if the pause appears by itself.

PAUSE

Your worry has a theme song now. Unfortunate, but useful.
Take the rhythm of the looping sentence and hum it without words for five seconds. Say the sentence normally once.

modes.rule: Guess whether the sentence keeps the same authority when the words disappear.
modes.play: Take the rhythm of the looping sentence and hum it without words for five seconds. Say the sentence normally once.

modes.mindBend: A thought is partly meaning—and partly just a noise pattern your mouth can hum.
modes.why: Language can feel inseparable from truth until its sound and meaning are pulled apart.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the sound gentle and comfortable—no loud volume or forced pitch. Stop if your throat or ears hurt, you feel dizzy, or breathing becomes uncomfortable.

PAUSE

Your foot apparently has topography.

See whether contact becomes a gradient instead of one blob.

modes.rule: Guess where your foot or hand presses hardest against the surface.

modes.twist: See whether contact becomes a gradient instead of one blob.

modes.why: Fine-grained sensation appears when attention stops using one global label.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Make the posture or pressure change small and pain-free; do not force range or hold a position that causes numbness, dizziness or discomfort.

modes.safety:
PAUSE

Free visual ghost, zero haunting required.
Look at a safe non-glare coloured object for five seconds, then shift to a plain surface and notice any brief ghost of colour or shape. Don’t stare at bright lights.
Guess whether a bright simple object leaves any trace when you look away.
See the trace fade without you doing anything.
modes.goal: Your eyes can keep a picture after the picture is gone.
modes.rule: Guess whether a bright simple object leaves any trace when you look away.
modes.play: Look at a safe non-glare coloured object for five seconds, then shift to a plain surface and notice any brief ghost of colour or shape. Don’t stare at bright lights.
modes.twist: See the trace fade without you doing anything.
modes.mindBend: What you experience now can include residue from what was there a moment ago.
modes.why: Perception can outlast the stimulus that triggered it.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Do not intensify the visual effect by staring harder or using brighter light. Use a comfortable object only and stop for pain, headache, dizziness or lingering visual change.

modes.why: Attention makes selected features feel more present without creating them.
modes.safety:
PAUSE

modes.characterLine: Your eyes have been editing around tiny black frames.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eyes have been editing around tiny black frames.

Guess how many blinks happen in twenty seconds.
Catch the fact that perception feels continuous despite repeated gaps.
modes.goal: Your world goes dark repeatedly and you barely notice.
modes.rule: Guess how many blinks happen in twenty seconds.
modes.play: For 20 sec, notice each blink as a tiny visual cut—no need to change the rate. Count only if easy.
modes.twist: Catch the fact that perception feels continuous despite repeated gaps.
modes.mindBend: Continuous experience is partly a very convincing edit.
modes.why: The brain stitches interruptions into a stable scene.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Blink gently at your natural pace—do not squeeze, hold the eyes shut or repeat the exercise to chase an effect. Stop if you get eye pain, marked dryness, dizziness or unusual visual symptoms.

modes.safety:
PAUSE

Catch the moment the unchanging thing becomes less available.
modes.goal: Your eyes are about to prove they stop reporting things that stay still.
modes.rule: Guess whether a fixed edge stays equally vivid when you stare beside it for ten seconds.

modes.twist: Catch the moment the unchanging thing becomes less available.
modes.mindBend: Something can stay present while your brain quietly stops shouting about it.
modes.why: Sensory systems prioritise change over perfect continuous reporting.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the chosen example as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

Your hands just conducted peer review.
Let both hands rest. Without moving much, compare finger curl, pressure, temperature, and weight left versus right. Soften only the tenser side by five percent.
Guess which hand is holding more unnecessary effort.
Notice how comparison reveals effort that felt invisible alone.

modes.safety:
PAUSE

modes.twist: Notice any shift in size, shape, weight, or vividness.

modes.why: The brain builds body experience from multiple senses that do not always agree perfectly.
modes.safety:
PAUSE

modes.displayName: NEXT BREATH IS NOT A COPY
modes.openingLine: Breathing refused to copy-paste.
modes.characterLine: Breathing refused to copy-paste.
modes.ritualCard:
Breathing refused to copy-paste.
Observe three natural breaths without changing them. Note one tiny difference in each: length, depth, pause, route, chest/belly movement.
Guess whether the next three breaths will be identical in depth and speed.
See whether the body repeats itself less exactly than expected.
modes.goal: Your last breath is trying to predict the next one.
modes.rule: Guess whether the next three breaths will be identical in depth and speed.
modes.play: Observe three natural breaths without changing them. Note one tiny difference in each: length, depth, pause, route, chest/belly movement.
modes.twist: See whether the body repeats itself less exactly than expected.
modes.mindBend: Your next breath does not have to obey the last one.
modes.why: Biological rhythms vary from cycle to cycle.
modes.returnPrompt: ↻ NEXT BREATH IS NOT A COPY
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Observe the three breaths exactly as they arrive. Do not hold, deepen, slow or lengthen pauses to create differences; stop if you feel faint, dizzy, more breathless or more panicked.

modes.play: Roll a sheet of paper into a tube. Look through it with one eye at a distant object. Hold your other open hand beside the tube, close to the far end. Keep both eyes open.
modes.twist: Catch the apparent hole through your palm where the tube view merges with the hand view.
modes.mindBend: A unified visual world can contain pieces that never existed together.
modes.why: The brain combines information from two eyes into one best-guess scene.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep this pass to one brief experiment. If it starts making you less steady, more confused or more stuck, stop and return to the concrete facts in front of you. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

modes.openingLine: Nearby object just won a tiny race.
modes.characterLine: Nearby object just won a tiny race.
modes.ritualCard:
Nearby object just won a tiny race.
Pick one nearby object aligned with a farther object. Move your head gently left and right while looking at both.
Guess which object appears to shift more when you move side to side: near or far.
Notice the near object seems to slide more across the background.
modes.goal: Move your head and the world reveals depth without changing position.
modes.rule: Guess which object appears to shift more when you move side to side: near or far.
modes.play: Pick one nearby object aligned with a farther object. Move your head gently left and right while looking at both.
modes.twist: Notice the near object seems to slide more across the background.
modes.mindBend: Depth is partly calculated from how the scene moves across you.
modes.why: Relative image motion is one cue the brain uses to infer distance.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the head movement small, slow and comfortable, with stable support nearby if needed. Stop with neck pain, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbance or any balance change.

Make a small triangle with your hands and centre a distant object inside it with both eyes open. Close one eye, then the other.
Guess which eye your brain trusts more for aiming.
Notice which eye keeps the object centred.
modes.goal: Two eyes, one tiny executive decision.
modes.rule: Guess which eye your brain trusts more for aiming.
modes.play: Make a small triangle with your hands and centre a distant object inside it with both eyes open. Close one eye, then the other.
modes.twist: Notice which eye keeps the object centred.
modes.mindBend: Two equal-looking sensors can contribute differently to one experience.
modes.why: Binocular vision often has a dominant eye for alignment tasks.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Close only one eye briefly and stay stationary while depth perception changes. Do not do this while driving, walking on stairs or doing anything that needs full binocular vision; stop for eye strain or dizziness.

PAUSE
